name: Thirumeniazhagar Temple, Tirumayendirapalli
deity: Shiva as Thirumeniazhagar (the Lord beautiful of form), with the goddess Vadivambikai
period: Ancient Shaiva shrine of Chola Nadu, sung in the Tevaram (7th century); structural temple with medieval and later additions
summary: Thirumeniazhagar is the beautiful Lord of the Tirumayendirapalli praised by Sambandar in the Tevaram, a quiet riverside shrine on the southern bank of the Kollidam where Indra is said to have worshipped and where the sun's rays touch the linga each Panguni.

sections.history: Tirumayendirapalli, today the village of Mayendrapalli, lies on the southern bank of the Kollidam, a short distance from the river's meeting with the sea, in the delta country north of the main Kaveri. The saint Tirugnanasambandar praised the Lord of this place in a decad of the Tevaram, and its verses recall the worship offered here by Surya, Chandra, Brahma and Indra, which is why the shrine counts among the Paadal Petra Sthalams. The place-name preserves the memory of Mahendra, the king of the gods, who is believed to have worshipped Shiva here, and the word palli in the name marks a sacred dwelling of the Lord. The present temple is a structural stone shrine raised and renewed by the medieval patrons of the Chola country, and worship has continued here without a break.
sections.architecture: The temple faces east beneath a three-tiered rajagopuram, and the sacred pool known as the Mahendra Theertham lies in front of it. Within the enclosure the sanctum of Thirumeniazhagar holds the Shiva linga, and the goddess Vadivambikai is honoured in her own shrine. The courtyard carries smaller shrines to Vinayaka, Kasi Viswanathar, Vishnu, Bhairava, Surya and Chandra, as well as a Nataraja shrine where he is worshipped with Sivakami and beside the saint Manikkavacakar. There is no separate Navagraha shrine here; instead Rahu and Ketu are placed beside Vinayaka. The sanctum is aligned so that the rays of the sun fall upon the linga on several days of the month of Panguni.
sections.legends: Tradition tells that Indra, called Mahendra, came to this quiet place on the Kollidam to be freed from a grievous curse, and worshipped Shiva after bathing in the tank that now bears his name. Pleased with his devotion, the Lord appeared to him in the beauty that gives the temple its name, Thirumeniazhagar, the Lord of the lovely form. Devotees hold that anyone who bathes in the Mahendra Theertham and worships the Lord here for forty-eight consecutive days is released from long-standing ailments and afflictions. The Tevaram verses also recall that Surya, Chandra and Brahma worshipped here, and the sun's own homage to the Lord is remembered each spring when his rays reach the linga.
sections.festivals: The special festival of the temple is the Surya Puja of Panguni, in March or April, when the rays of the sun fall on the linga for about seven days and the Lord is worshipped with great devotion. Maha Shivaratri, Panguni Uthiram, Margazhi Tiruvadirai and the Tirukarthikai lamp festival are kept in the traditional way, and the monthly Pradosham is observed as at every Shiva temple. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: Mayendrapalli rewards a visitor who comes without haste. The village is small and the road to it passes through green delta fields, and the temple keeps the stillness of a place far from the busy highways. Pause at the Mahendra Theertham before entering, then stand before Thirumeniazhagar and, in the days of Panguni, notice how the morning light is made part of the worship. The goddess Vadivambikai is then honoured in her own shrine. Those who come to pray for health often return for the forty-eight days, and for many families this unhurried shrine of the Tevaram is a place of private and lasting devotion.

visit.timings: Typically open for a few hours in the morning and again in the early evening, with a long midday break; timings vary between sources, so confirm locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: The temple is about 7 km from Aachalpuram (Tirunallur Perumanam) on the road from Chidambaram to Sirkazhi: cross the Kollidam bridge and take the branch road to Aachalpuram and Mayendrapalli. Buses run to the area from Chidambaram and Sirkazhi, and Sirkazhi is the nearest convenient railway station. Services to the village itself are infrequent, so hiring a car or auto-rickshaw from Sirkazhi is the easiest way to arrive.
